title: Why Is My HVAC System Making Noise?
h1: Why Is Your HVAC System Making Noise?
description: HVAC noises like banging, squealing, rattling or hissing point to different problems. Learn what each sound usually means and which need a technician fast.
quick_answer: Some HVAC sound is normal, like a soft hum or a whoosh of air. New or louder noises usually mean something is loose, worn or restricted. Banging and rattling often point to loose parts or ducts, squealing to a belt or motor, clicking to controls, and hissing to an air or refrigerant leak. The sound tells you where to look.
body:
Your heating and cooling system makes some noise every time it runs. You hear the blower start, air move through the vents and the outdoor unit hum. What matters is change. A new sound, or a familiar one that's suddenly louder, is often the first sign of a problem, and catching it early can keep a small fix from becoming a big repair.

What do common HVAC noises mean?

NoiseCommon causes
Banging or clankingA loose or broken part in the blower, a loose motor mount, or ducts expanding and contracting
RattlingLoose panels or screws, debris in the outdoor unit, or loose ductwork
Squealing or screechingA worn blower belt on older systems, motor bearings, or a failing fan motor
ClickingNormal at start and stop. Constant clicking can mean a relay, control board or ignition problem
Buzzing or humming loudlyAn electrical issue, a failing capacitor, or a motor that's struggling to start
HissingAir leaking from ducts, or a refrigerant leak near the coil or lines
WhistlingA restricted filter, closed vents or a return that's too small
Gurgling or bubblingCondensate drain issues or, sometimes, a refrigerant problem
Booming at furnace start-upDelayed ignition from dirty burners, which needs prompt service

Which noises need attention right away?

Turn the system off and call for service if you hear:

  • A loud bang or boom when the furnace starts. This can be delayed ignition, where gas builds up before lighting. It can damage the heat exchanger over time.
  • Screaming or a very high-pitched whine. This can mean high pressure in the compressor or a serious refrigerant problem.
  • Grinding or metal-on-metal sounds. Motor bearings may be failing.
  • Loud buzzing with no start-up. A motor or compressor may be trying to start and can't.

If you smell gas along with any noise, leave the house and call your gas utility from outside. If a carbon monoxide alarm goes off, get everyone out and call 911.

What noises are normal?

A soft click when the thermostat calls for heat or cooling, a short whoosh as the furnace lights, a steady hum from the outdoor unit and the sound of air moving through vents are all normal. Ducts can also tick or pop as they warm up and cool down, especially metal ducts in attics on cool mornings.

What can I check myself?

  1. Replace the filter. A clogged filter causes whistling and makes the blower louder.
  2. Open all supply vents and clear the returns.
  3. Look at the outdoor unit for leaves, sticks or debris in the fan area. Turn off power at the disconnect before clearing anything.
  4. Check for loose screws on access panels and grilles.
  5. Note when the noise happens: at start-up, while running or at shutdown. This helps a technician find the cause faster.

Leave anything involving gas, refrigerant, capacitors or wiring to a technician. These parts can be dangerous to handle.

Why is my outdoor unit so loud?

Outdoor units get louder as fan blades wear, motors age or debris builds up. A failing capacitor can cause a hard, buzzy start. Coastal homes can see faster corrosion on panels and fasteners from salt air, which leads to rattles. Santa Ana winds can also blow debris into the unit. A yearly tune-up keeps the outdoor unit cleaner and catches worn parts early.

Does an older system make more noise?

Usually. Motors, bearings and fan blades wear with age, and older furnaces often use belt-driven blowers that squeal as belts stretch. Newer variable-speed equipment tends to run quieter because it ramps up slowly instead of starting at full speed. If an older system has grown noticeably louder, it's a good time for a full inspection.

Can ducts be noisy?

Yes. Ducts can pop, rattle or whistle. Popping usually comes from metal expanding and contracting. Rattling can mean loose hangers or connections. Whistling often points to undersized ducts or returns, or to air leaking through gaps. Sealing and securing ducts usually quiets them down.

Our HVAC technicians diagnose and repair noisy systems across San Diego County and Orange County. If the noise seems to come from the ducts, our air duct team can inspect, secure and seal them.
faqs: Is it normal for my HVAC to make noise when it turns on?
A soft click, a short whoosh from the burner and the sound of the blower ramping up are normal. A bang, boom, screech or grinding sound at start-up is not, and should be checked.
Why does my furnace bang when it turns on?

A bang at start-up is often delayed ignition, where gas builds up before it lights, usually because of dirty burners. It can also be ducts flexing. Delayed ignition needs prompt service, so turn the furnace off and call a technician.
Why is my AC making a hissing sound?

Hissing can come from air leaking out of the ducts or from a refrigerant leak. If cooling is weaker than usual or there's ice on the lines, a refrigerant leak is likely and needs a certified technician.
Can a dirty filter make my HVAC louder?
Yes. A clogged filter makes the blower work harder and can cause whistling at the return grille. Replacing the filter is the easiest first step when the system gets louder.
